01 / The supported argument

Cooperation survived the violence.

The strongest case concerns Ambedkar’s willingness to approve continued political cooperation with the League after Calcutta, and the practical cooperation of organisations associated with his movement.

The central question has two parts: what political choices were made after the killings, and who can be held responsible for each choice? A personal instruction carries greater weight for Ambedkar’s position than a provincial leader’s speech or a joint procession.

The evidence below lets the reader assess a serious criticism: whether pursuit of representation and safeguards justified maintaining this relationship after the violence. That judgment should rest on the documented choices, with the participants’ stated reasons kept visible.

The case for continued cooperation is stronger than the case for endorsement of the specific 16 August programme or its killings. These are separate propositions; evidence for one cannot simply be substituted for evidence for the other.

E01Direct documentAmbedkar2 June 1947Bengal

Explicit approval: work in alliance with the League

Exact excerpt
In the meantime I agree that you should work in alliance with the League and secure adequate safeguards for them

Spelling normalised: the reproduced edition prints “allianee”. No words have been omitted within this excerpt.

Surrounding context · editorial summary

Confidential letter to Mandal, replying to 30 May. Ambedkar considered Scheduled Castes unable to impose or prevent partition. Their course was safeguards in either a united or divided Bengal. Eastern Bengal residents might remain after partition; migration and land in Western Bengal were also considered.

He sent his safeguards memorandum for negotiations and allowed additional local demands. He saw a possible advantage in the League’s support for separate electorates, while stating that Muslims were no greater friends of Scheduled Castes than Hindus.

What this supportsPersonal approval of practical cooperation after Calcutta and Noakhali, with an accompanying negotiation brief.

Scope & qualificationThe immediate subject is safeguards, especially for Eastern Bengal. This is not an instruction for the August 1946 programme or approval of its violence.

Government of Maharashtra; reprinted by Dr. Ambedkar Foundation · Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, vol. 17, part I (2003 / 2014)
Printed pp. 362–364; especially p. 363 · item 39 · PDF viewer page 405

Source trail: BAWS credits Khairmode, vol. 8, pp. 164–166. Sen discusses this letter at pp. 185–186 of his 2018 book.

E02Reported approvalAmbedkarOctober 1946National

Approval of Mandal’s League-sponsored government appointment

Evidence · editorial summary

Mandal says that Suhrawardy conveyed the offer of an Interim Government position in October 1946. He accepted on condition that he could resign if Ambedkar disapproved, and reports receiving approval by telegram from London.

The separate published trail for the approval runs through Jagadish Mandal, Mahapran Jogendranath, p. 90, and a 29 October 1946 letter to D. G. Jadhav, cited by Anirban Bandyopadhyay, “Orchestrating a Signal Victory,” p. 57, n.94. Those originals remain unread; related transmission means these accounts should not automatically be counted as independent witnesses.

What this supportsA first-person account connecting Ambedkar to acceptance of a League-sponsored office after Calcutta.

Scope & qualificationThe witness wrote in 1950. This is testimony about the telegram; the telegram itself has not been independently inspected.

Committee of Enquiry, Indian Commission of Jurists, New Delhi · Recurrent Exodus of Minorities from East Pakistan and Disturbances in India (1965; Appendix IV reproduces Mandal’s letter of 9 October 1950)
Appendix IV, printed p. 355, paragraph 4 · PDF viewer page 371

Source trail: Mandal’s resignation letter, headed 9 October 1950, reproduced by the Indian Commission of Jurists in 1965. The original London telegram is still not independently inspected. Further bibliography: Anirban Bandyopadhyay’s chapter in Biswamoy Pati, ed., Invoking Ambedkar (Primus, 2014), pp. 33–57, especially p. 57 n.94; original letter uninspected.

E03First-person testimonyMandal1946 events · testimony of 9 October 1950Bengal

Mandal acknowledges continuing despite atrocities

Exact excerpt
The terrible sufferings of Hindus overwhelmed me with grief, but still I continued the policy of co-operation with the Muslim League.
Surrounding context · editorial summary

Mandal recalls the Calcutta killings, demands for his resignation and threats to his life. He then describes killings, forced conversions, rape, abductions and losses in Noakhali, including suffering among Scheduled Castes. He acknowledges maintaining cooperation despite those events.

The surrounding account also says he appealed to Scheduled Castes to remain outside the communal bloodshed. The inspected 1965 passage does not contain the sometimes-circulated claim that four Anglo-Indian and four Scheduled Caste votes alone saved the ministry; this edition does not repeat it as verified.

What this supportsDirect first-person acknowledgment that knowledge of atrocities did not end Mandal’s League partnership.

Scope & qualificationRetrospective testimony, reproduced in 1965. It establishes Mandal’s continued political cooperation, while his account describes an appeal against participation in communal fighting. Ambedkar’s personal responsibility requires his own correspondence or evidence of approval.

Committee of Enquiry, Indian Commission of Jurists, New Delhi · Recurrent Exodus of Minorities from East Pakistan and Disturbances in India (1965; Appendix IV reproduces Mandal’s letter of 9 October 1950)
Appendix IV, printed p. 355, paragraph 3 · PDF viewer page 371

Source trail: Date and original printed pagination verified in the 1965 volume: heading on p. 354, relevant paragraph on p. 355. This supersedes the date ambiguity in the modern reproduction previously used.

E05Archival scholarshipFederationNovember 1946Bengal

League and Federation leaders issued a joint appeal

Evidence · editorial summary

Sen records a joint appeal signed by Nazimuddin, Fazlur Rahman, Moazzem Hossain, Abul Hashim, Mandal, Rasik Lal Biswas, Bholanath Biswas and Dwarika Nath Baruri, sustaining their alliance and urging peace.

The November pamphlet also proposed joint committees at village, union and thana levels. Further citation: Bandyopadhyay and Chaudhury (2017), p. 250, nn.92–93; WBSA IB File 717D-46, abstract 16 November 1946. The originals are not independently inspected.

What this supportsOrganised cooperation after Calcutta and Noakhali.

Scope & qualificationThe appeal’s stated object included preventing further violence. Ambedkar was not a signatory.

E08Historical reconstructionFederation15 August 1946Bengal

Joint mobilisation immediately before Direct Action Day

Evidence · editorial summary

Sen dates the Federation’s Anti-Poona Pact Day to 15 August. He describes a joint Federation–League procession and a meeting presided over by Mandal, calling for common action and invoking Ambedkar and Jinnah.

The source trail includes Star of India, 13–14 August, and S.B.D.N., 21 August 1946, WBSA IB File 191/46. Oxford’s later description places participation on 16 August while citing Sen’s account of 15 August. This is a source-dependent dating conflict, not independent corroboration.

What this supportsA demonstrable political connection between the two movements in the immediate run-up to 16 August.

Scope & qualificationDo not silently change this date to 16 August or treat a speaker’s invocation of Ambedkar as a personal order from him.

Dwaipayan Sen · The Decline of the Caste Question: Jogendranath Mandal and the Defeat of Dalit Politics in Bengal (Cambridge University Press, 2018)
Printed pp. 139–140; notes 4–7

Source trail: Star of India, 13 August 1946; subsequent newspaper and intelligence references in Sen. Other scholarship’s dating must be compared rather than harmonised without evidence.

E09Published interviewAmbedkar17 July 1946National

Conditional support for a League struggle against the British

Exact excerpt
If the Muslim League starts any direct struggle against the British—I fully support the stand taken by the Sikhs at present—then they will also get our support in their action.

User-supplied image 1. The intervening reference to Sikhs is retained; no ellipsis removes the stated anti-British condition.

Surrounding context · editorial summary

Ambedkar offered support if the League began a direct struggle against the British. Federation satyagraha had begun at Poona on 15 July.

What this supportsPrior willingness to cooperate against the Cabinet Mission settlement.

Scope & qualificationThis predates the League’s 29 July Direct Action resolution. Shared terminology does not establish a shared operational plan.

Muslim alignment remained a possible political option

Exact excerpt
I have not given advice to that effect

User-supplied image 8. The denial concerns advice already given, not rejection of a possible future change.

Surrounding context · editorial summary

Ambedkar denied already advising conversion to Islam but left possible Muslim alignment open if separate representation failed.

E11Contemporary reporting via historianFederation16 October 1946Delhi · Bombay / Poona · UP · Nagpur / CP & Berar · Bengal

Public gratitude to Jinnah after the killings

Evidence · editorial summary

Sen records celebrations in several cities and about 3,000 Scheduled Caste men thanking Jinnah for Mandal’s nomination.

Reported celebrations included Agra, Fatehgarh, Calcutta, Delhi, Bombay and Nagpur. Their local organisers and dates are not all supplied. The Delhi gathering is specifically dated 16 October; it should not be assumed that every participant was an enrolled SCF member.

What this supportsPublic political gratitude after Calcutta.

Scope & qualificationThese participants cannot stand for every Scheduled Caste person or prove Ambedkar organised the demonstrations.

E14Proceedings · page image checkedFederation30 July 1947Punjab

Punjab: a Federation president supported the League-aligned advocate in court

Exact excerpt
supported Mr. Salig Ram

Short exact excerpt from the transcript’s parenthetical record of support; the two named supporters are identified in the surrounding summary.

Surrounding context · editorial summary

On p. 430, Salig Ram identifies Chaudhri Sukh Lal as president of the Pakistan Scheduled Castes Federation and says he and Sardar Hari Singh Ramdasia are present in court. On p. 431, the proceedings record both men supporting Salig Ram in court.

This is stronger evidence than an advocate merely asserting authority: named leaders were present and supported him during the hearing. The source names a specific Pakistan Federation body, rather than establishing a mandate from every provincial Federation or Ambedkar.

What this supportsIdentifiable Federation leadership backed the presentation favouring alignment with Muslims well after August 1946.

Scope & qualificationThe passage does not establish an instruction from Ambedkar, an All-India Federation resolution, or participation in communal violence.

E15Proceedings · page image checkedFederation30 July 1947Punjab

League counsel introduced and defended Salig Ram’s appearance

Evidence · editorial summary

At the opening of the day’s hearing, Sir Muhammad Zafrullah Khan arranged time for the Scheduled Caste representative alongside his other submissions. On p. 430 he introduced Salig Ram and defended his appearance after commissioners challenged his credentials.

Zafrullah Khan said he had personally checked with the president and secretary of the Depressed Classes League. Those office-bearers should not be silently conflated with the Pakistan Scheduled Castes Federation president separately identified later on the page.

What this supportsPractical coordination of a Scheduled Caste presentation with League counsel in the boundary proceedings.

Scope & qualificationCoordination in this hearing is direct evidence of political/legal cooperation. It does not establish financing, central SCF authorisation or a violent operational alliance.

E16Proceedings · page image checkedFederation30 July 1947Punjab

A substantive boundary argument for placing Scheduled Castes with Muslims

Exact excerpt
the interests of the Scheduled Castes lie in the fact that they should be put together with the Muslims.
Surrounding context · editorial summary

Salig Ram advocated separate representation as protection against caste exclusion. He disputed the representative standing of legislators elected with caste-Hindu votes. On p. 434 he praised the League for nominating Mandal from its own Interim Government quota and praised Jinnah’s advocacy of Scheduled Caste interests.

He portrayed treatment in Muslim villages as better and used that claim to support the territorial and political conclusion quoted above. On p. 431 he also mentioned letters from Mandal and other Depressed Class members; their dates and full contents are not reproduced there. Those references cannot be treated as Mandal’s specific authorisation of this submission.

What this supportsA League-aligned territorial argument, presented with Federation leaders’ recorded support after the Calcutta and Noakhali violence.

Scope & qualificationThe transcript proves that these arguments were made; it does not independently validate claims about Muslim village life. Nor does it prove that Mandal’s mentioned letters endorsed the boundary demand.

E17Essential primary-source contextFederationJuly 1947 hearingsPunjab

The Punjab position was contested by other Scheduled Caste representatives

Evidence · editorial summary

Rai Bahadur Badri Dass presented an opposing Scheduled Caste case, identified legislators supporting his representation and submitted village resolutions against the rival memorandum. Commissioners later challenged Salig Ram’s credentials.

On p. 430 Justice Mahajan reported a petition alleging that Salig Ram had been promised a public-prosecutor position. This is a reported allegation, not a judicial finding of bribery. On p. 201 Badri Dass described Ambedkar as aligned with the Indian Constituent Assembly; that is the advocate’s assertion, not a personal statement by Ambedkar.

What this supportsThe pro-League presentation represented an identifiable leadership group within a contested political field.

Scope & qualificationDo not describe every Punjab Scheduled Caste legislator or community as supporting Pakistan. Do not convert an allegation against counsel into an established fact.

Mandal publicly praised Jinnah in Pakistan’s inaugural Assembly

Exact excerpt
the greatest statesman and one of the greatest men of the world today.
Surrounding context · editorial summary

Speaking as temporary chairman at the first meeting of Pakistan’s Constituent Assembly, Mandal expressed gratitude and admiration for Jinnah. He presented Pakistan’s creation as the outcome of a legitimate minority demand and expressed confidence in its future treatment of minorities.

The speech is affirmative public praise nearly a year after Direct Action Day, rather than merely an inference from continued officeholding. His confidence in Pakistan is part of his stated political position, not this dossier’s assessment of the promises’ fulfilment.

What this supportsPublic political confidence in Jinnah and Pakistan after the 1946 violence.

E26Published evidence · attributedFederation15 July–18 September 1946Bombay / Poona · Nagpur / CP & Berar

The SCF campaign had its own chronology in Poona, Wardha and Nagpur

Evidence · editorial summary

The campaign began at Poona on 15 July; a CP Assembly demonstration followed on 18 July. Poona action was suspended on 28 July. Demonstrations followed at Wardha on 8 August and renewed Nagpur action from 2 September, with a lathi charge on 18 September. The article reports 7,777 arrests during the September movement.

Independent contemporary check: Indian Annual Register, July–December 1946, II, printed pp. 6–7 records the July Poona and CP demonstrations, including approximately 10,000 at the CP Assembly. Printed p. 9 records later League decisions. Source AR provides the scan.

What this supportsA substantial movement extending across the pre- and post-16 August periods.

Scope & qualificationArrests need not represent distinct people; the campaign’s existence alone does not show support for communal attacks.

04 / Claims & confidence

How far does the evidence go?

PropositionAssessmentRead
Ambedkar approved political cooperation after the killings.Direct documentary support; define the alliance’s immediate scope.E01, E02
Mandal continued despite awareness of atrocities.Explicit retrospective acknowledgment.E03
Federation bodies continued practical cooperation.Supported by events, appeals and documented campaigning.E04–E07
Punjab Federation leadership supported a League-aligned boundary presentation after August 1946.Verified in the proceedings; central All-India authorisation remains unestablished.E14–E17
UP SCF supported League demands after the killings.Archival scholarship identifies specific reports; original CID pages not obtained.E18–E19
Ambedkar endorsed the specific 16 August programme or ensuing killings.Not established by the documents assembled here.E08, E09
The League alone supplied his decisive Assembly votes.Stronger claim than the verified electoral evidence allows.E12
Political cooperation proves religious admiration for Islam.A conclusion about personal conviction needs additional evidence.E10, E13

Political responsibility can be criticised without claiming operational responsibility for a riot. To make the argument precise, identify the decision, its date, the political benefit sought, and the evidence linking it to Ambedkar personally.

Continued cooperation permits scrutiny of priorities and judgment. It does not by itself tell us whether a participant accepted an ally’s explanation of violence, considered all alternatives worse, or believed negotiation could protect vulnerable people. Those explanations must be established, not supplied by assumption.

06 / Editorial method

Read critically. Cite precisely.

What counts as a quotation?

Only shaded blocks labelled “Exact excerpt” reproduce source language. Surrounding explanations are editorial summaries. Short excerpts are selected for the specific proposition; use the linked pages to inspect the full document. E01 discloses a spelling normalisation. E14 uses a short excerpt from a parenthetical record of support; E19 quotes through Rawat. No quotation is invented to fill a gap.

What do the evidence labels mean?

A direct document records the author’s own instruction. Reported approval is another person’s testimony about an instruction. Contemporary reporting may still be mediated by a later compilation. Archival scholarship identifies and interprets sources that have not necessarily been independently inspected for this edition. These distinctions matter more than a single numerical confidence score.

Why retain qualifications in a critical dossier?

A narrowly supported accusation is harder to dismiss than an expansive one resting on inference. The qualifications identify where an opponent could fairly challenge attribution, chronology or source access. They accompany copied citations so that an excerpt retains its evidentiary scope.

Unresolved checks and further research
  • Locate the original London approval telegram and the 29 October 1946 Jadhav letter.
  • Inspect the Jinnah Papers funding correspondence at the exact pages identified in E07.
  • Compare the original newspaper reports behind the 15/16 August dating issue.
  • Obtain original UP weekly intelligence entries dated 30 August, 20 and 27 September, 18 October and 6 December 1946; record original page and paragraph numbers.
  • Inspect Punjab compilation volume I, pp. 142–149 and 420; do not confuse these distinct documents with letters mentioned in volume II.
  • Verify electoral records before assigning individual Constituent Assembly votes.
  • Any claim of approval of the killings requires a specific, attributable document; neither silence nor later alliance alone supplies it.
